claim: Application of the HCN channel blocker ZD7288 (30 µM) decreased the conduction velocity by 8.0 ± 2.8% in myelinated cerebellar mossy fibers (n = 14).
source: Application of the specific HCN channel blocker ZD7288 (30 µM) decreased the conduction velocity by 8.0 ± 2.8% in myelinated cerebellar mossy fibers (n = 14), by 9.2 ± 0.9% in unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (n = 15), and by 4.0 ± 0.8% in optic nerves (n = 4; see Figure 1 and its legend for statistical testing).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in cerebellar mossy fibers before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in the text and Figure 1.

claim: Application of ZD7288 (30 µM) decreased the conduction velocity by 9.2 ± 0.9% in unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (n = 15).
source: Application of the specific HCN channel blocker ZD7288 (30 µM) decreased the conduction velocity by 8.0 ± 2.8% in myelinated cerebellar mossy fibers (n = 14), by 9.2 ± 0.9% in unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (n = 15), and by 4.0 ± 0.8% in optic nerves (n = 4; see Figure 1 and its legend for statistical testing).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in parallel fibers before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in the text and Figure 1.

claim: Application of ZD7288 (30 µM) decreased the conduction velocity by 4.0 ± 0.8% in optic nerves (n = 4).
source: Application of the specific HCN channel blocker ZD7288 (30 µM) decreased the conduction velocity by 8.0 ± 2.8% in myelinated cerebellar mossy fibers (n = 14), by 9.2 ± 0.9% in unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (n = 15), and by 4.0 ± 0.8% in optic nerves (n = 4; see Figure 1 and its legend for statistical testing).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in optic nerves before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in the text and Figure 1.

claim: ZD7288 at 30 µM did not affect voltage-dependent Na+ currents in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
source: As some studies implied that ZD7288 might have unspecific side effects, such as blocking voltage-dependent Na+ channels (Chevaleyre and Castillo, 2002; Wu et al., 2012), we recorded Na+ currents from 53 cMFBs and found no change in the amplitude or kinetics of voltage-dependent Na+ currents after ZD7288 application (Figure 1—figure supplement 1),suggesting that under our conditions and at a concentration of 30 µM, ZD7288 did not affect the Na+ currents.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental recordings of Na+ currents from 53 cMFBs showing no change in amplitude or kinetics after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Application of 8-Br-cAMP (500 µM) increased the conduction velocity by 5.9 ± 2.8% in cerebellar mossy fibers (n = 17).
source: The conduction velocity increased by 5.9 ± 2.8% in cerebellar mossy fibers (n = 17), by 3.7 ± 1.4% in parallel fibers (n = 10), and by 4.6 ± 0.6% in optic nerves (n = 5; see Figure 1 and its legend for statistical testing).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in cerebellar mossy fibers before and after 8-Br-cAMP application, as shown in the text and Figure 1.

claim: Application of 8-Br-cAMP (500 µM) increased the conduction velocity by 3.7 ± 1.4% in parallel fibers (n = 10).
source: The conduction velocity increased by 5.9 ± 2.8% in cerebellar mossy fibers (n = 17), by 3.7 ± 1.4% in parallel fibers (n = 10), and by 4.6 ± 0.6% in optic nerves (n = 5; see Figure 1 and its legend for statistical testing).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in parallel fibers before and after 8-Br-cAMP application, as shown in the text and Figure 1.

claim: Application of 8-Br-cAMP (500 µM) increased the conduction velocity by 4.6 ± 0.6% in optic nerves (n = 5).
source: The conduction velocity increased by 5.9 ± 2.8% in cerebellar mossy fibers (n = 17), by 3.7 ± 1.4% in parallel fibers (n = 10), and by 4.6 ± 0.6% in optic nerves (n = 5; see Figure 1 and its legend for statistical testing).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in optic nerves before and after 8-Br-cAMP application, as shown in the text and Figure 1.

claim: HCN channels control the conduction velocity in both myelinated and unmyelinated central axons.
source: These results indicate that HCN channels control the conduction velocity in both myelinated and unmyelinated central axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that ZD7288 and 8-Br-cAMP modulate conduction velocity in myelinated mossy fibers, unmyelinated parallel fibers, and optic nerves.

claim: Application of 200 µM norepinephrine resulted in a 1.9 ± 0.8% increase in conduction velocity in cerebellar parallel fibers (n = 6).
source: Application of 200 µM norepinephrine (NE) resulted in a relatively fast increase in conduction velocity (1.9 ± 0.8%; n = 6; see Figure 2A and C–E; see legend for statistical testing), consistent with the existence of β-adrenergic receptors in the cerebellar cortex (Nicholas et al., 1993) that increase the cAMP concentration via Gs-proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in parallel fibers before and after norepinephrine application, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Application of 200 µM serotonin resulted in a –3.5 ± 0.5% decrease in conduction velocity in cerebellar parallel fibers (n = 11).
source: On the other hand, the application of either 200 µM serotonin (–3.5 ± 0.5%; n = 11), 200 µM dopamine (–5.0 ± 0.7%; n = 13) or 200 µM adenosine (–7.2 ± 0.6%; n = 5) resulted in a continuous decrease of the conduction velocity (Figure 2B and C–E), consistent with the existence of Gi-coupled receptors for serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine in the molecular layer of the cerebellum (Geurts et al., 2002; Schweighofer et al., 2004), which decrease the cAMP concentration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in parallel fibers before and after serotonin application, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Application of 200 µM dopamine resulted in a –5.0 ± 0.7% decrease in conduction velocity in cerebellar parallel fibers (n = 13).
source: On the other hand, the application of either 200 µM serotonin (–3.5 ± 0.5%; n = 11), 200 µM dopamine (–5.0 ± 0.7%; n = 13) or 200 µM adenosine (–7.2 ± 0.6%; n = 5) resulted in a continuous decrease of the conduction velocity (Figure 2B and C–E), consistent with the existence of Gi-coupled receptors for serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine in the molecular layer of the cerebellum (Geurts et al., 2002; Schweighofer et al., 2004), which decrease the cAMP concentration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in parallel fibers before and after dopamine application, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Application of 200 µM adenosine resulted in a –7.2 ± 0.6% decrease in conduction velocity in cerebellar parallel fibers (n = 5).
source: On the other hand, the application of either 200 µM serotonin (–3.5 ± 0.5%; n = 11), 200 µM dopamine (–5.0 ± 0.7%; n = 13) or 200 µM adenosine (–7.2 ± 0.6%; n = 5) resulted in a continuous decrease of the conduction velocity (Figure 2B and C–E), consistent with the existence of Gi-coupled receptors for serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine in the molecular layer of the cerebellum (Geurts et al., 2002; Schweighofer et al., 2004), which decrease the cAMP concentration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of conduction velocity in parallel fibers before and after adenosine application, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Physiological neuromodulators can both increase and decrease action potential conduction velocity, depending on the type of neuromodulator and receptor.
source: These data nevertheless indicate that physiological neuromodulators can both increase and decrease action potential conduction velocity, depending on the type of neuromodulator and receptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that norepinephrine increases conduction velocity while serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine decrease it.

claim: The effects of cAMP and neuromodulators on conduction velocity are mainly mediated by HCN channels.
source: This was not significantly different from the decrease measured in the presence of ZD7288 alone (control, –3.3 ± 1.4%; n = 7, see Figure 2G), indicating that the previously shown effects of cAMP and neuromodulators on conduction velocity are mainly mediated by HCN channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that when HCN channels are blocked with ZD7288, neuromodulators no longer affect conduction velocity, as shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Cerebellar mossy fiber boutons exhibit a substantial voltage sag in response to hyperpolarizing current injections.
source: Injection of depolarizing currents during current-clamp recordings evoked a single action potential, while injection of hyperpolarizing currents generated a substantial 'sag' (Figure 3B; Rancz et al., 2007; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014) (i.e. a delayed depolarization towards the resting potential, which is a hallmark of the presence of Ih) (Biel et al., 2009; Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by current-clamp recordings from cMFBs showing a voltage sag in response to hyperpolarizing current injections, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At a potential of approximately –150 mV, the sag ratio in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was 0.497 ± 0.030 (n = 12).
source: At a potential of, on average, –150 mV, the sag ratio (calculated from the peak and steady state amplitude as indicated in Figure 3C (George et al., 2009) was 0.497 ± 0.030 (n = 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of the sag ratio from current-clamp recordings in cMFBs, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The amplitude and half-duration of action potentials elicited at 1 Hz in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons were not significantly affected by the application of 30 µM ZD7288.
source: In both cases, the amplitude and half-duration of the action potentials elicited at 1 Hz were not significantly affected by the application of 30 µM ZD7288 (data not shown and Figure 4B and C, respectively), indicating that HCN channels do not alter the active membrane properties profoundly.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of action potential amplitude and half-duration before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: HCN channels do not alter the active membrane properties of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons profoundly.
source: In both cases, the amplitude and half-duration of the action potentials elicited at 1 Hz were not significantly affected by the application of 30 µM ZD7288 (data not shown and Figure 4B and C, respectively), indicating that HCN channels do not alter the active membrane properties profoundly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ZD7288 does not significantly affect action potential amplitude and half-duration at 1 Hz.

claim: Blocking HCN channels significantly impaired the ability of mossy fibers to fire at high frequencies.
source: Blocking HCN channels significantly impaired the ability of mossy fibers to fire at high frequencies (20 stimuli at 200–1666 Hz).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced failure-free firing frequency in the presence of ZD7288, as shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The average failure-free frequency in cerebellar mossy fibers was reduced from 854 ± 60 Hz under control conditions to 426 ± 63 Hz in the presence of ZD7288 (n = 20 and 10, respectively; PT-Test = 0.0002).
source: The average failure-free frequency was reduced from 854 ± 60 Hz under control conditions to 426 ± 63 Hz in the presence of ZD7288 (n = 20 and 10, respectively; PT-Test = 0.0002; Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of failure-free firing frequency in cMFBs before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: HCN channels ensure reliable high-frequency firing in cerebellar mossy fibers.
source: These experiments show, that HCNs, despite their slow kinetics, ensure reliable high-frequency firing.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that blocking HCN channels reduces the maximal failure-free firing frequency and increases action potential failures during high-frequency trains.

claim: ZD7288 caused a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs, n = 94 and 35, respectively).
source: ZD7288 caused (i) a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs n = 94 and 35, respectively), (ii) a doubling of the apparent input resistance calculated from the steady-state voltage at the end of the current step (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ, respectively), and (iii) a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant, as determined by a mono-exponential fit to the initial decay of the membrane potential (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms, respectively; see legend of Figure 5B for statistical testing).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of resting membrane potential in cMFBs before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ZD7288 caused a doubling of the apparent input resistance in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs, respectively).
source: ZD7288 caused (i) a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs n = 94 and 35, respectively), (ii) a doubling of the apparent input resistance calculated from the steady-state voltage at the end of the current step (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ, respectively), and (iii) a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant, as determined by a mono-exponential fit to the initial decay of the membrane potential (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms, respectively; see legend of Figure 5B for statistical testing).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of apparent input resistance in cMFBs before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ZD7288 caused a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs, respectively).
source: ZD7288 caused (i) a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs n = 94 and 35, respectively), (ii) a doubling of the apparent input resistance calculated from the steady-state voltage at the end of the current step (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ, respectively), and (iii) a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant, as determined by a mono-exponential fit to the initial decay of the membrane potential (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms, respectively; see legend of Figure 5B for statistical testing).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of apparent membrane time constant in cMFBs before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Adding cAMP in various concentrations to the intracellular solution depolarized the membrane potential and decreased both the input resistance and the apparent membrane time constant in a concentration-dependent manner in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
source: Adding cAMP in various concentrations to the intracellular solution depolarized the membrane potential and decreased both the input resistance and the apparent membrane time constant in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of membrane potential, input resistance, and membrane time constant with different intracellular cAMP concentrations, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HCN channels in cerebellar mossy fibers determine the passive membrane properties as a function of the intracellular cAMP concentration.
source: These data suggest that HCN channels in cerebellar mossy fibers determine the passive membrane properties as a function of the intracellular cAMP concentration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both ZD7288 and varying intracellular cAMP concentrations affect passive membrane properties in opposite directions.

claim: HCN2 is the dominating subunit in cerebellar mossy fibers.
source: In addition, immunogold-electron microscopy revealed HCN2 as the dominating subunit in cerebellar mossy fibers.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy showing significant labeling for HCN2 but only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 in cMFBs, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: Immunogold labeling revealed only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
source: At the electron microscopic level, we found only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 (data not shown) but significant labeling for HCN2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy showing no significant HCN1 labeling in cMFBs.

claim: Immunogold labeling revealed significant labeling for HCN2 in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
source: At the electron microscopic level, we found only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 (data not shown) but significant labeling for HCN2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy showing significant HCN2 labeling in cMFBs, as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HCN2 immunogold particles were diffusely distributed along the plasma membrane of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, with similar labeling density in the adjacent mossy fiber axon.
source: HCN2 immunogold particles were diffusely distributed along the plasma membrane of cMFBs, with similar labeling density in the adjacent mossy fiber axon (Figure 6B), which could be traced back up to 3.5 µm from cMFBs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy showing diffuse distribution of HCN2 particles along the plasma membrane of cMFBs and adjacent axons, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HCN2 was uniformly distributed without apparent spatial relations to synapses in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
source: HCN2 was uniformly distributed without apparent spatial relations to those synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D reconstruction of a cMFB showing uniform distribution of HCN2 gold particles without spatial clustering near synapses, as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The density of immunogold particles for HCN2 in a reconstructed cerebellar mossy fiber bouton was 17.1 particles/µm2 (in total 1260 particles per 73.65 µm2).
source: The density of immunogold particles for HCN2 in this reconstructed bouton was 17.1 particles/µm2 (in total 1260 particles per 73.65 µm2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunogold particles in a 3D reconstructed cMFB.

claim: The mean density of immunogold particles for HCN2 in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was 22.7 ± 2.4 per μm2 (n = 6 cMFBs from two mice).
source: The mean density of immunogold particles for HCN2 was 22.7 ± 2.4 per μm2 (n = 6 cMFBs from two mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunogold particles across multiple cMFBs.

claim: HCN2 is the dominant subunit mediating Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, consistent with its pronounced cAMP-dependence.
source: These data indicate that HCN2 is the dominant subunit mediating Ih in cMFBs, consistent with its pronounced cAMP-dependence.
evidence: The claim is inferred from immunogold labeling showing predominant HCN2 expression and the observed strong cAMP-dependence of Ih in cMFBs.

claim: Hyperpolarizing voltage steps evoked a slowly activating, non-inactivating inward current in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, which was inhibited by ZD7288.
source: Hyperpolarizing voltage steps evoked a slowly activating, non-inactivating inward current, which was inhibited by ZD7288 (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings from cMFBs showing slowly activating, non-inactivating inward currents that are blocked by ZD7288, as shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The mean V½ of Ih activation in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was –103.3 ± 0.8 mV (n = 36).
source: Using the tail currents of ZD7288-sensitive currents evoked by voltage steps between –80 mV and –150 mV from a holding potential of –70 mV, we calculated the activation curve of Ih with a mean V½ of –103.3 ± 0.8 mV (Figure 7B; n = 36 V½-values, each from a different cMFB).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of tail currents from voltage-clamp recordings in cMFBs, as shown in Figure 7B.

claim: About 7% of the overall HCN2-mediated current is active at rest in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
source: On the basis of the average resting membrane potential of cMFBs, this means that about 7% of the overall HCN2-mediated current is active at rest.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the V½ of Ih activation and the average resting membrane potential of cMFBs.

claim: With 1 mM cAMP, V½ of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons shifted by 17 mV to, on average, –86.6 ± 1.2 mV (n = 16 cMFBs; PT-Test <10−10).
source: With 1 mM cAMP, V½ shifted by 17 mV to, on average, –86.6 ± 1.2 mV (n = 16 cMFBs; PT-Test <10−10; Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings from cMFBs with 1 mM cAMP in the intracellular solution, as shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The EC50 of intracellular cAMP for the shift in V½ of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons is 40.4 µM.
source: The resulting average shifts of V½ revealed an EC50 of 40.4 µM intracellular cAMP (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of V½ shifts at different intracellular cAMP concentrations, as shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Under perforated patch conditions, the V½ of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was –96.4 ± 1.2 mV (n = 10), significantly more depolarized than the corresponding whole-cell recordings after rupture of the perforated patch (–101.3 ± 1.0 mV; n = 10; PT-Test = 0.0076).
source: Under perforated patch conditions, the V½ of Ih was –96.4 ± 1.2 mV (n = 10), significantly more depolarized than the corresponding whole-cell recordings after rupture of the perforated patch (–101.3 ± 1.0 mV; n = 10; PT-Test = 0.0076; Figure 7C; see Materials and methods for comparisons with additional control groups).
evidence: The claim is supported by perforated patch recordings from cMFBs compared to whole-cell recordings, as shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The endogenous cAMP concentration in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons is 12.6 µM, with a 68% confidence interval of 1.8 to 60.7 µM cAMP.
source: This voltage shift (4.9 ± 1.2 mV, n = 10 cMFBs) indicates an endogenous cAMP concentration of 12.6 µM in cMFBs, with a 68% confidence interval of 1.8 to 60.7 µM cAMP (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the voltage shift observed in perforated patch recordings and the EC50 of cAMP for Ih activation, as shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The reversal potential of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was –23.4 ± 1.4 mV (n = 7).
source: Furthermore, we estimated the reversal potential of Ih with short voltage ramps as described previously (Cuttle et al., 2001) and found a value of –23.4 ± 1.4 mV (n = 7; Figure 8C), similar to previous estimates (Aponte et al., 2006; Cuttle et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements using voltage ramps in cMFBs, as shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The depolarization caused by HCN2 channels controls conduction velocity in cerebellar mossy fibers.
source: The results showed that the Vm-model but not the Rm-model caused an increase in conduction velocity, indicating that the depolarizing effect of axonal HCN2 channels determines conduction velocity (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that only the model simulating depolarization (Vm-model) but not the model simulating decreased membrane resistance (Rm-model) increased conduction velocity, as shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Increasing the resting membrane potential from –90 mV to –65 mV decreased the availability of voltage-dependent Na+ channels but increased the conduction velocity in the computational model.
source: Interestingly, increasing the resting membrane potential from –90 mV to –65 mV, decreased the availability of voltage-dependent Na+ (NaV) channels but increased the conduction velocity (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that depolarization increases conduction velocity despite decreasing Na+ channel availability, as shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The conduction velocity decreased only at resting membrane potentials above –65 mV in the computational model.
source: The conduction velocity decreased only at resting membrane potentials above –65 mV in our model.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing a non-linear relationship between resting membrane potential and conduction velocity, as shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The depolarization mediated by HCN2 channels accelerates the conduction velocity by bringing the membrane potential closer to the firing threshold.
source: Together, these data indicate that the depolarization mediated by HCN2 channels accelerates the conduction velocity by bringing the membrane potential closer to the firing threshold.
evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling showing that depolarization, not decreased membrane resistance, increases conduction velocity.

claim: It is approximately 100% more expensive to maintain the resting membrane potential with Ih than without or by depolarization alone in the computational model.
source: Computational modeling showed that it is ~100% more expensive to maintain the resting membrane potential with Ih than without or by depolarization alone (Vm-model; Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling of ATP consumption required to maintain the resting membrane potential, as shown in Figure 9F.

claim: The metabolic cost of maintaining the resting membrane potential with Ih for one second was approximately 3-fold higher than the cost of generating one action potential in the computational model.
source: Furthermore, the metabolic cost of maintaining the resting membrane potential with Ih for one second was ~3-fold higher than the cost of generating one action potential (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling of ATP consumption for maintaining resting potential versus generating action potentials, as shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Assuming an average frequency of cerebellar mossy fibers of 4 Hz in vivo, the HCN2 channels increased the required energy of cerebellar mossy fibers by approximately 30%.
source: Assuming an average frequency of cerebellar mossy fibers of 4 Hz in vivo (Chadderton et al., 2004; Rancz et al., 2007), the HCN2 channels increased the required energy of cerebellar mossy fibers by ~30%.
evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling of ATP consumption and literature values for average firing frequency in vivo.

claim: HCN channels are a major consumer of the energetic demands of axons.
source: These data indicate that HCN2 channels are a major consumer of the energetic demands of axons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling showing high metabolic costs of HCN channels for maintaining resting membrane potential.

claim: HCN channels increase action potential velocity and fidelity in central axons.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the HCN channels increase action potential velocity and fidelity in central axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that HCN channels increase conduction velocity and ensure reliable high-frequency firing.

claim: HCN channels control conduction velocity primarily by altering the resting membrane potential.
source: Computational modeling indicated that HCN2 channels control conduction velocity primarily by altering the resting membrane potential and are associated with significant metabolic costs.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that the Vm-model but not the Rm-model reproduces the effects of HCN channels on conduction velocity.

claim: HCN channels are associated with significant metabolic costs.
source: Computational modeling indicated that HCN2 channels control conduction velocity primarily by altering the resting membrane potential and are associated with significant metabolic costs.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing high ATP consumption for maintaining resting membrane potential with HCN channels.

claim: The cAMP-HCN pathway provides neuromodulators with an opportunity to finely tune energy consumption and temporal delays across axons in the brain.
source: These results suggest that the cAMP-HCN pathway provides neuromodulators with an opportunity to finely tune energy consumption and temporal delays across axons in the brain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing neuromodulator effects on conduction velocity and computational modeling showing metabolic costs of HCN channels.

claim: HCN channels are expressed in the heart and nervous system and comprise four members (HCN1–HCN4).
source: HCN channels are expressed in the heart and nervous system and comprise four members (HCN1–HCN4), which differ in their kinetics, voltage-dependence and degree of sensitivity to cyclic nucleotides such as cAMP (Biel et al., 2009; Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HCN1–HCN4 differ in their kinetics, voltage-dependence and degree of sensitivity to cyclic nucleotides such as cAMP.
source: HCN channels are expressed in the heart and nervous system and comprise four members (HCN1–HCN4), which differ in their kinetics, voltage-dependence and degree of sensitivity to cyclic nucleotides such as cAMP (Biel et al., 2009; Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Membrane hyperpolarization activates HCN channels and causes a depolarizing mixed sodium/potassium (Na+/K+) current.
source: Membrane hyperpolarization activates HCN channels and causes a depolarizing mixed sodium/potassium (Na+/K+) current.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about HCN channel function.

claim: In the heart, the current through HCN channels (If) mediates the acceleratory effect of adrenaline on heart rate by direct binding of cAMP.
source: In the heart, the current through HCN channels (If) mediates the acceleratory effect of adrenaline on heart rate by direct binding of cAMP (DiFrancesco, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In neurons, the current through HCN channels (Ih) controls a wide array of functions, such as rhythmic activity and excitability.
source: In neurons, the current through HCN channels (Ih) controls a wide array of functions, such as rhythmic activity (Pape and McCormick, 1989) and excitability (Tang and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HCN channels are expressed throughout various subcellular compartments of neurons.
source: In addition to the somatic impact, HCN channels are expressed throughout various subcellular compartments of neurons (Nusser, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Patch-clamp recordings from dendrites in pyramidal neurons have revealed particularly high densities of HCN channels that act to control the local resting potential and leak conductance.
source: For example, patch-clamp recordings from dendrites in pyramidal neurons have revealed particularly high densities of HCN channels that act to control the local resting potential and leak conductance, thereby playing important roles in regulating synaptic integration (George et al., 2009; Harnett et al., 2015; Kole et al., 2006; Magee, 1999; Williams and Stuart, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ih seems to control the strength of synaptic transmission in the crayfish and the Drosophila neuromuscular junction.
source: Ih seems to control the strength of synaptic transmission in the crayfish and the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (Beaumont and Zucker, 2000; Cheung et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Presynaptic recordings from the vertebrate calyx of Held in the auditory brainstem found Ih to only have a marginal effect on neurotransmitter release.
source: However, presynaptic recordings from the vertebrate calyx of Held in the auditory brainstem found Ih to only have a marginal effect on neurotransmitter release (Cuttle et al., 2001), but to exert a strong influence on the resting membrane potential (Cuttle et al., 2001; Kim and von Gersdorff, 2012) and on vesicular neurotransmitter uptake (Huang and Trussell, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At the synaptic terminals of pyramidal neurons in the cortex of mice, HCN channels inhibit glutamate release by suppressing the activity of T-type Ca2+ channels.
source: At the synaptic terminals of pyramidal neurons in the cortex of mice, HCN channels inhibit glutamate release by suppressing the activity of T-type Ca2+ channels (Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In axons of the stomatogastric nervous system of lobsters, the action potential conduction was affected by dopamine acting via axonal HCN channels.
source: Indeed, in axons of the stomatogastric nervous system of lobsters (Marder and Bucher, 2001), the action potential conduction was affected by dopamine acting via axonal HCN channels (Ballo et al., 2010; Ballo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Studies on action potential propagation by Waxman and coworkers indicated that Ih counteracts the hyperpolarization of the membrane potential during periods of high-frequency firing.
source: In vertebrates, studies on action potential propagation by Waxman and coworkers indicated that Ih counteracts the hyperpolarization of the membrane potential during periods of high-frequency firing (Baker et al., 1987; Birch et al., 1991; Waxman et al., 1995), and that it participates in ionic homeostasis at the node of Ranvier (Waxman and Ritchie, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ih is crucial for the emergence of persistent action potential firing in axons of parvalbumin-positive interneurons.
source: More recent investigations found Ih to be crucial for the emergence of persistent action potential firing in axons of parvalbumin-positive interneurons (Elgueta et al., 2015), but Ih seems to have an opposing effect on the excitability at the axon initial segment, where its activation reduces the probability of action potential initiation (Ko et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: There is evidence from extracellular recordings that blocking Ih decreases the action potential conduction velocity in unmyelinated central axons and peripheral axons of vertebrates.
source: Finally, there is evidence from extracellular recordings that blocking Ih decreases the action potential conduction velocity in unmyelinated central axons (Baginskas et al., 2009; Soleng et al., 2003) and peripheral axons of vertebrates (Grafe et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The neuromodulation of conduction velocity and the underlying cellular membrane mechanisms are not known in vertebrate axons.
source: However, the neuromodulation of conduction velocity and the underlying cellular membrane mechanisms are not known in vertebrate axons.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in knowledge based on the absence of prior studies.

claim: Cerebellar mossy fibers can conduct trains of action potentials at frequencies exceeding 1 kHz.
source: However, cerebellar mossy fibers can conduct trains of action potentials at frequencies exceeding 1 kHz (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014), making them an ideal target to investigate the impact of axonal HCNs on the propagation of high-frequency action potentials.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: HCN1 and HCN2 are predominantly expressed in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Of the four HCN subunits (HCN1–HCN4), the subunits HCN1 and HCN2 are predominantly expressed in the cerebellar cortex (Notomi and Shigemoto, 2004; Santoro et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies in the cortex, hippocampus, and auditory brainstem primarily detected HCN1 in axons.
source: Previous studies in the cortex, hippocampus, and auditory brainstem primarily detected HCN1 in axons (Elgueta et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2016), but HCN2 was found to be more sensitive to cAMP than HCN1 (Wang et al., 2001; Zagotta et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HCN2 was found to be more sensitive to cAMP than HCN1.
source: Previous studies in the cortex, hippocampus, and auditory brainstem primarily detected HCN1 in axons (Elgueta et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2016), but HCN2 was found to be more sensitive to cAMP than HCN1 (Wang et al., 2001; Zagotta et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The changes in baseline conduction velocity mediated by HCN channels are relatively small, in the range of approximately 5%.
source: We describe both an increase and decrease of the baseline axonal conduction velocity in the range of ~5% mediated by HCN channels (Figures 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Figures 1-3.

claim: HCN channels can be expected to change the arrival time of the action potential by, for example, 0.5 ms in the case of unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (assuming 3 mm length and 0.3 m/s velocity).
source: Although the changes in baseline conduction velocity are relatively small, considering the long distances that axons traverse in the brain, HCN channels can be expected to change the arrival time of the action potential by, for example, 0.5 ms in the case of unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (assuming 3 mm length and 0.3 m/s velocity; Swadlow and Waxman, 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data on conduction velocity changes and literature values for axon length and velocity.

claim: Temporal delays caused by HCN channels will influence information processing in the central nervous system, because spike-timing dependent plasticity, coincidence detection, and the neuronal rhythms of cell ensembles precisely tune the arrival times of action potentials.
source: Such temporal delays will influence information processing in the central nervous system, because spike-timing dependent plasticity (Caporale and Dan, 2008), coincidence detection (Softky, 1994), and the neuronal rhythms of cell ensembles (Buzsáki et al., 2013) precisely tune the arrival times of action potentials.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data on conduction velocity changes and citations to literature on spike-timing dependent processes.

claim: The cerebellum is involved in the accurate control of muscle contraction with a temporal precision of 1–100 ms.
source: The cerebellum is involved in the accurate control of muscle contraction with a temporal precision of 1–100 ms (Hore et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Submillisecond correlations in spike timing occurring between neighboring Purkinje cells have been noted previously.
source: Submillisecond correlations in spike timing occurring between neighboring Purkinje cells have been noted previously (reviewed in Isope et al., 2002; Person and Raman, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Submillisecond precision of the mossy or parallel fiber input are critical for information processing in the cerebellar circuits.
source: Furthermore, submillisecond precision of the mossy or parallel fiber input are critical for information processing in the cerebellar circuits (Braitenberg et al., 1997; Heck et al., 2001; Isope et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The here-described changes in action potential conduction velocity in mossy and parallel fibers may play an important role in cerebellar computation.
source: Together, the here-described changes in action potential conduction velocity in mossy and parallel fibers (Figures 1–3) may thus play an important role in cerebellar computation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data and literature on cerebellar function.

claim: The view of the axon as a cable-like compartment in which conduction velocity is static has substantially changed over recent years in favor of a model that allows flexibility and complex forms of axonal computation.
source: Indeed, the view of the axon as a cable-like compartment in which conduction velocity is static has substantially changed over recent years in favor of a model that allows flexibility and complex forms of axonal computation (Debanne et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Axon diameters change during long-term potentiation.
source: Recent findings showed that axon diameters change during long-term potentiation (Chéreau et al., 2017), and changes in myelination in the motor cortex were resolved during the learning of complex motor skills (McKenzie et al., 2014; for environmental effects on myelination see also Forbes and Gallo, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Changes in myelination in the motor cortex were resolved during the learning of complex motor skills.
source: Recent findings showed that axon diameters change during long-term potentiation (Chéreau et al., 2017), and changes in myelination in the motor cortex were resolved during the learning of complex motor skills (McKenzie et al., 2014; for environmental effects on myelination see also Forbes and Gallo, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The control of conduction velocity is solely mediated by changes in resting membrane potential.
source: Our analysis revealed that the control of conduction velocity is solely mediated by changes in resting membrane potential.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that only the Vm-model but not the Rm-model affects conduction velocity.

claim: Isolated changes in membrane conductance and thus in the membrane time and length constant had no effect on conduction velocity.
source: Isolated changes in membrane conductance and thus in the membrane time and length constant had no effect on conduction velocity (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that the Rm-model does not affect conduction velocity, as shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The increased conduction velocity upon depolarization is consistent with a previously observed correlation between conduction velocity and the depolarization from the resting potential required to reach the firing threshold in motoneurons.
source: The increased conduction velocity upon depolarization is consistent with a previously observed correlation between conduction velocity and the depolarization from the resting potential required to reach the firing threshold in motoneurons (Carp et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results and citation to previous literature.

claim: The modeling results are in agreement with the nonlinear cable theory predicting that the difference between the resting membrane potential and the firing threshold is a critical parameter for action potential conduction velocity.
source: Interestingly, these findings are in agreement with the nonlinear cable theory predicting that the difference between the resting membrane potential and the firing threshold is a critical parameter for action potential conduction velocity (see, for example, Figure 12.25 in Jack et al. (1983) which shows increasing velocity with increasing safety factor, that is, decreasing excitation threshold 'VB').
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results and citation to previous literature.

claim: Ca2+ entering through axonal voltage-gated Ca2+ channels could interact with the cAMP pathway by activating or inhibiting different subtypes of adenylyl cyclase and phosphodiesterase.
source: Interestingly, Ca2+ entering through axonal voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Brenowitz and Regehr, 2007) could interact with the cAMP pathway by activating or inhibiting different subtypes of adenylyl cyclase and phosphodiesterase (Bruce et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The extent to which conduction failures occur under physiological conditions is controversial.
source: The extent to which conduction failures occur under physiological conditions is controversial (Debanne et al., 2011; Rama et al., 2018; Radivojevic et al., 2017), but our data indicate that HCN channels are required to ensure the reliable initiation and conduction of action potentials at high frequencies.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature indicating controversy.

claim: HCN channels are required to ensure the reliable initiation and conduction of action potentials at high frequencies.
source: The extent to which conduction failures occur under physiological conditions is controversial (Debanne et al., 2011; Rama et al., 2018; Radivojevic et al., 2017), but our data indicate that HCN channels are required to ensure the reliable initiation and conduction of action potentials at high frequencies.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced failure-free firing frequency when HCN channels are blocked.

claim: Ih counteracts the hyperpolarization during high-frequency firing.
source: This is consistent with Ih counteracting the hyperpolarization during high-frequency firing (Waxman et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous literature.

claim: The evolutionary design of HCN channels as a continuously open shunt for Na+ influx incurs significant metabolic costs.
source: Our modeling results (Figure 9) indicate that the evolutionary design of HCN channels as a continuously open shunt for Na+ influx incurs significant metabolic costs.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling of ATP consumption.

claim: A metabolically cheaper way to depolarize the membrane would be the expression of fewer Na+-K+-ATPases, resulting in a depolarized K+ reversal potential.
source: These high costs might appear surprising, because a metabolically cheaper way to depolarize the membrane would be the expression of fewer Na+-K+-ATPases, resulting in a depolarized K+ reversal potential (cf. Vm-model in Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling comparing different mechanisms of depolarization.

claim: The endogenous cAMP concentration in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons is higher than previous estimates of 50 nM in Aplysia sensory neurons and 1 µM in cardiomyocytes.
source: This is higher than previous estimates of 50 nM in Aplysia sensory neurons (Bacskai et al., 1993; but see Greenberg et al., 1987) and 1 µM in cardiomyocytes (Börner et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim compares the measured endogenous cAMP concentration to values from previous literature.

claim: A recently reported low cAMP-sensitivity of protein kinase A argues for high intracellular cAMP concentrations.
source: But a recently reported low cAMP-sensitivity of protein kinase A (Koschinski and Zaccolo, 2017), a prototypical cAMP-regulated protein, also argues for high intracellular cAMP concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: High cAMP concentrations may be limited to spatially restricted domains.
source: On the other hand, our data do not rule out that such high cAMP concentrations are limited to spatially restricted domains.
evidence: The claim is speculative and acknowledges limitations of the data.

claim: Local cAMP signaling-compartments were recently observed in Drosophila axons.
source: The possibility of local cAMP signaling-compartments was recently observed in Drosophila axons (Maiellaro et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A high endogenous cAMP concentration and expression of the HCN2 isoform facilitates the ability of neuromodulators to control conduction velocity bidirectionally and dynamically.
source: A high endogenous cAMP concentration and expression of the HCN2 isoform facilitates the ability of neuromodulators to control conduction velocity bidirectionally and dynamically.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data on cAMP-dependence and neuromodulator effects.

claim: Gs-coupled receptors for serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine are expressed in the molecular layer of the cerebellum.
source: Indeed, Gs-coupled receptors for serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine are expressed in the molecular layer of the cerebellum (see, for example, Geurts et al., 2002; Schweighofer et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Adenosine has been shown to be an endogenous sleep factor.
source: Interestingly, adenosine, which decreased the conduction velocity (Figure 2), has been shown to be an endogenous sleep factor (Basheer et al., 2004; Porkka-Heiskanen et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine play important regulatory functions during sleep in the cerebellum.
source: Moreover, serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine play important regulatory functions during sleep in, for example, the cerebellum (Canto et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The cAMP-HCN pathway in axons could contribute to the reduced energy consumption of the brain during sleep.
source: The cAMP-HCN pathway in axons could thus contribute to the reduced energy consumption of the brain during sleep (Boyle et al., 1994; Townsend et al., 1973).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other mechanisms, such as direct influences on voltage-dependent Na+, K+, and Ca2+ channels, could contribute to the modulation of conduction velocity.
source: Nevertheless, other mechanisms, such as direct influences on voltage-dependent Na+ (Yin et al., 2017), K+ (Yang et al., 2013), and Ca2+ channels (Burke et al., 2018), could contribute to the modulation of conduction velocity.
evidence: The claim acknowledges alternative mechanisms and is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Off-target interactions cannot be excluded with the used concentrations of neuromodulators.
source: Furthermore, off-target interactions cannot be excluded with the used concentrations of neuromodulators.
evidence: The claim acknowledges limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: The function of HCN channels has been studied in human peripheral nerves using non-invasive threshold tracking techniques.
source: The function of HCN channels has been studied in human peripheral nerves using non-invasive threshold tracking techniques (Howells et al., 2016; Howells et al., 2012; Lorenz and Jones, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Significant alterations of HCN channel expression and/or function have been described in pathologies such as stroke, porphyria, diabetic neuropathy, neuropathic pain, and inflammation.
source: Significant alterations of HCN channel expression and/or function have been described in pathologies such as stroke (Jankelowitz et al., 2007), porphyria (Lin et al., 2008), diabetic neuropathy (Horn et al., 1996), neuropathic pain (Chaplan et al., 2003), and inflammation (Momin and McNaughton, 2009), as well as in a vertebrate model of demyelination (Fledrich et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HCN channels seem to be causally related to pain symptoms.
source: Furthermore, HCN channels seem to be causally related to pain symptoms (Chaplan et al., 2003; Momin and McNaughton, 2009) and therapeutic blockade of HCN channels are also considered (Wickenden et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HCN could play a compensatory role in restoring conduction velocity in some diseases.
source: On the basis of our findings, HCN could also play a compensatory role in restoring conduction velocity in some diseases.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the experimental findings.
